questions.prompt: Wahaj keeps a release number that people increase by hand. A teammate edits Nabd's tool schema and forgets to increase it. Which practice would have shown the change?
options: A manifest whose release id is a hash of every part
A stricter reminder in the team's release checklist
Running the evaluation set once a month
Keeping the release number in the prompt file
questions.explanation: A content hash changes whenever any part changes, whether or not anyone remembered to bump a number.
misconceptions: Relies on memory, the thing that failed
Detects a behaviour change late and does not say which part changed
Moves the number without making it follow the content

questions.prompt: Nabd's release names a provider alias that ends in "latest". What should each call's log record so that a silent model change shows up in a diff?
options: The prompt text only
The model identifier returned in the response
The alias the release asked for
The number of tokens of the answer
questions.explanation: The response names the model that actually served the call; the alias can point at a different snapshot tomorrow.
misconceptions: Assumes the prompt is the only part that can change behaviour
Records the pointer, which looks the same before and after it moves
Records a symptom that varies for many reasons

questions.prompt: Nabd's prompt, model and tools are unchanged, but the manuals index was rebuilt with a revised manual. Is this a new release?
options: No: only the data changed, not the system
No, unless the answers get worse
Yes: the index is part of what changes behaviour
Only if the index is larger than before
questions.explanation: The retrieval index decides which text the model sees, so a rebuilt index is a change to the release unit.
misconceptions: Treats the retrieval index as data outside the release
Decides by outcome after the fact instead of by what changed
Ties the release to size instead of content

questions.prompt: You retrain the champion from its registry lineage. Which evidence proves you reproduced it?
options: The same AUC on the holdout to three decimals
The same number of trees in both models
The same file name for the training data
The same data hash, the same code hash and identical predictions row by row
questions.explanation: Equal inputs (data and code hashes) and equal outputs (every prediction) are the proof; a metric alone is not.
misconceptions: Two different models can share a metric
Shape is not behaviour
A file name says nothing about its rows

questions.prompt: A retraining script reads the champion's parameters back from the tracking store and passes them straight to the trainer. It fails on the sample weight. Why?
options: The tracking store returns parameters as strings
The champion was trained with a different library
The registry deleted the parameter after promotion
Sample weights cannot be logged
questions.explanation: Parameters are stored as text, so code that retrains from the registry converts each one back to its type.
misconceptions: Guesses at the environment before reading the error
Parameters stay with the run
Confuses logging with typing

questions.prompt: A monthly batch arrives with one region's load written as a fraction. Which design stops it doing harm?
options: Train, then reject the model if its AUC falls
A contract step before training that stops the run and reports the column
A cleaning step that rescales small loads
Let the crews report odd inspection lists
questions.explanation: The contract names the broken column before any model learns from it and sends the report to the owner of the source.
misconceptions: A model trained and scored on broken data can still score well
Repairs a fault the data owner has not confirmed
Detection after the damage, by the people it hurts

questions.prompt: Why does Lab 1.3 validate the batch lazily, collecting every failure?
options: It is faster than stopping at the first failure
Because pandera cannot stop at the first failure
So the data owner can fix every problem in one delivery
So the pipeline can repair the failing rows
questions.explanation: One report with every failure saves a round trip per problem with the team that owns the export.
misconceptions: Speed is not the reason
It can; lazy is a choice
Validation reports; it does not repair

questions.prompt: A challenger beats the champion overall and is 0.07 AUC worse in one region; the gate's tolerance is 0.03. What should the gate do?
options: Promote: the overall gain outweighs one region
Raise the tolerance for this release
Promote and watch that region closely
Reject it, and record the region and the reason
questions.explanation: The regional rule is set before the release; a loss far beyond the noise in one region blocks promotion.
misconceptions: Lets an average hide the people who pay for it
Changes the rule to pass a candidate
Ships a known regression and hopes a monitor catches it

questions.prompt: Why does the promotion gate allow a small drop in a region instead of none at all?
options: A region's AUC on a few hundred feeders varies by a few hundredths between samples
Small regions matter less to the company
Challengers are always slightly worse in some region
The champion's scores are rounded
questions.explanation: Without a tolerance the gate would reject almost every challenger on sampling noise; the bootstrap measures its size.
misconceptions: Treats a fairness rule as a business weight
Not a law; it is noise
Rounding is far smaller than the tolerance

questions.prompt: Serving loads models:/fault-risk@champion. What is the release when challenger B passes the gate?
options: Copy B's model file into the service image
Move the champion alias to B, keep previous-champion on the old version, tag the reason
Delete the old champion version
Retrain B on all data and register it
questions.explanation: Moving an alias is one recorded, reversible change; the previous version stays one move away.
misconceptions: Bypasses the registry and loses the audit record
Removes the rollback
Ships a model the gate never saw

questions.prompt: Staging tested Nabd's image yesterday. Today the production job builds the image again from the same commit and deploys it. Why is this a problem?
options: The commit may have been changed since yesterday
A second build takes longer than a deploy
The production build may differ from what staging tested
Production needs a different tag than staging
questions.explanation: Only the digest that passed staging is known to work; a rebuild can pull newer base images or packages.
misconceptions: Commits are immutable; base images and packages are not
Treats the issue as speed, not identity
A different tag is still a different build

questions.prompt: Dhafer wants production deploys of Nabd to need an approval that a pull request cannot remove. Where does he put the rule on GitHub?
options: In a step of the workflow file that waits for a comment
In a branch name convention
In the README of the repository
In the production environment's protection rules
questions.explanation: Required reviewers on the environment are repository settings, outside the files a pull request can change.
misconceptions: A pull request can edit the file and remove the step
Names do not stop a job from running
Documentation does not enforce anything

questions.prompt: Dhafer merged a change to Nabd and is also on the production reviewer list. Self-review is blocked. Who can approve the release?
options: Another listed reviewer, such as Mutab
Anyone in the team with write access
Dhafer, because he is a reviewer
Nobody: the release must be merged again by someone else
questions.explanation: One approval from a listed reviewer who did not merge lets the production job start.
misconceptions: Ignores the reviewer list
Ignores the self-review rule
Invents a rule; one other reviewer is enough

questions.prompt: A candidate release of Nabd changes the prompt and the model at once, and the gate blocks it. What is the main drawback of this release?
options: It costs more to evaluate
The result does not say which change caused the block
It must be rolled back twice
The gate cannot run on two changes
questions.explanation: Changing one part per release lets a gate result point at its cause.
misconceptions: Evaluation cost is the same for any candidate
A rollback restores the whole release at once
The gate runs; the problem is reading its result

questions.prompt: A cheaper model keeps answer correctness at 0.917 but completes 5 of 6 safety procedures. The gate has a floor of 1.00 on safety steps. What is the decision?
options: Ship: the overall score is unchanged
Ship to half the crews to compare
Block, and log the safety metric and the failing case
Rerun the gate until it passes
questions.explanation: A floor with no allowed drop blocks the release on one failure; the log names the metric and the case.
misconceptions: Lets an average decide a rule written as a floor
Exposes crews to an incomplete isolation procedure
Games the gate instead of fixing the model

questions.prompt: The platform team refreshes Nabd's manuals index without changing code, prompt or model. Should the refresh go through the evaluation gate?
options: Only if the number of chunks changes
No: no code changed
No: new manuals can only improve answers
Yes: it changes what the model reads
questions.explanation: The index decides the context; a refresh is a release and is gated like one.
misconceptions: Content can change with the same chunk count
Treats code as the only part that changes behaviour
A new section can outrank the right one or split a procedure

questions.prompt: At 5% the canary served 30 requests in its pause with no problems. The analysis's minimum sample is 50. What should happen?
options: Report inconclusive and extend the pause
Roll back
Advance to 25%
Lower the minimum sample for this release
questions.explanation: Below the minimum sample there is no evidence either way: wait, then hand the decision to a person.
misconceptions: Punishes low traffic instead of a problem
Treats a quiet window as evidence
Changes the rule to fit the data

questions.prompt: Why does the canary analysis compare the candidate's graded answers with the stable version's grades on the same requests rather than with last week's average?
options: Last week's average is not stored
The same requests remove the effect of a changing question mix
It makes the canary faster
The stable version is always right
questions.explanation: The question mix changes through the day; a paired comparison leaves only the difference between versions.
misconceptions: The issue is validity, not storage
Pairing does not change speed
The stable version is a baseline, not a truth

questions.prompt: A new model snapshot passed the offline gate and 30 minutes of shadow, then failed at 25% when the next shift asked mostly in Arabic. What should change before the next attempt?
options: Skip the shadow: it was misleading
Raise the latency objective
Add Arabic cases offline and shadow across a shift change
Go straight to 50% to get a larger sample
questions.explanation: A candidate is tested only on the traffic it sees; the instruments need traffic like the failing shift.
misconceptions: Removes a safe source of evidence
Moves the rule instead of the evidence
Exposes more users to a known failure

questions.prompt: A configuration halves Mubadir's cost per model call, but its resolved share drops from 0.70 to 0.40. About how does the cost per resolved report change?
options: It halves
It is unchanged
It doubles
It falls only slightly, and unresolved reports need a person
questions.explanation: 0.5 x 0.70 / 0.40 is about 0.88 of the old cost per success, before the extra human work.
misconceptions: Divides by calls, not outcomes
Ignores both the price and the success rate
Ignores that each call is cheaper

questions.prompt: Someone added the current date as the first line of Nabd's system prompt, and the cache hit rate fell from 0.62 to 0.12. Why?
options: Prompt caches match the start of a request, and the start now changes daily
The provider stopped caching dates
Dates make prompts longer
Cached tokens expire at midnight
questions.explanation: Stable text belongs first and changing text last, so the cached prefix stays the same.
misconceptions: Invents a provider rule
Length is not the cause
The cause is the changing prefix, not expiry

questions.prompt: A month-end forecast alert fires for the fault-risk classifier on the 7th; its spend jumped on the day of the planned monthly retrain. What is the best fix?
options: Remove budget alerts for the classifier
Forecast planned jobs separately from daily running cost
Raise the classifier's budget until the alert stops
Alert only on the last day of the month
questions.explanation: A planned job inside the forecast window inflates the projection; treat it as a known item.
misconceptions: Loses the signal for real overspend
Hides the cause behind a bigger number
Too late to act

questions.prompt: Finance asks why AI costs are shown per team instead of as one platform bill. What is the main reason?
options: It is required to move money between teams
It makes the total bill smaller
Teams decide their use, so seeing their own cost changes their choices
It hides the cost of the platform team
questions.explanation: Showback puts cost in front of the people who choose how much to use.
misconceptions: That is chargeback, not showback
Showing costs does not reduce them by itself
Showback is about visibility, not hiding
